explicit_propositions.text: The Continuing Resolution passed by Congress continues government funding at approximately current levels.
Discretionary spending accounts for about $1.7 trillion of the federal budget.
The federal government is projected to spend $7 trillion in the current fiscal year.
The federal government is expected to run a deficit of $1.8 trillion in the current fiscal year.
The Continuing Resolution resulted in a net reduction of $7 billion in spending compared to previous levels.
Of the $7 billion in savings, $13 billion was initially trimmed from discretionary spending before $6 billion was redirected to defense.
Non-discretionary spending—including Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid—totals approximately $3.8 to $4 trillion annually.
Interest payments on the national debt are estimated at nearly $950 billion this fiscal year.
The Debt Ceiling is expected to be reached in August, requiring Congress to raise it again.
A proposed 'one big beautiful bill' aims to consolidate tax, energy, border security, and debt ceiling reforms into a single piece of legislation.

assumptions.text: The public values the perception of fiscal responsibility even if actual cuts are minimal.
Symbolic actions like using a chainsaw metaphor generate political legitimacy even without significant structural change.
Government efficiency efforts are primarily intended to signal commitment rather than achieve deep structural reform.
Congressional leadership prioritizes maintaining political momentum over achieving transformative fiscal reductions.
The electorate equates visible action with progress, regardless of magnitude.
Raising the debt ceiling is politically unavoidable despite concerns about long-term fiscal sustainability.
Tax cuts expiring at the end of the year would cause significant economic harm to middle-class families.
Reciprocal tariffs are believed to promote fairness in international trade and benefit domestic manufacturing.
Public trust in government increases when officials appear proactive—even symbolically—on issues like waste and inefficiency.
Legislative outcomes are shaped more by political optics and coalition-building than by strict adherence to fiscal discipline.
